title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and pedagogically useful feedback from classroom transcripts. The authors focus on three teacher-coaching tasks for generative AI: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study evaluates gpt-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT) in zero-shot mode using the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset. The transcripts come from 1,660 elementary mathematics classroom observations collected from 317 teachers across four U.S. school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. For the qualitative tasks, the researchers recruited two experienced math teachers, including one instructional coach, to rate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty. For the scoring task, they compared model predictions with existing expert ratings on CLASS and MQI observation items.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT shows promise as a scalable feedback tool but performs poorly relative to human expert judgments. It has low correlations with human scores on observation items, often produces generic or redundant suggestions, and generates a nontrivial amount of unfaithful or hallucinated feedback. The paper argues that current generative AI should complement, not replace, human coaching, and highlights privacy, hallucination, and alignment concerns when using classroom transcripts for automated feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational language model used for zero-shot text generation and prediction.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot on three teacher-coaching tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On transcript scoring, ChatGPT showed low Spearman correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI dimensions (e.g., CLPC 0.00/0.04/-0.06; CLBM 0.35/0.23/0.07; CLINSTD -0.01/0.07/-0.05; EXPL 0.02/0.12/-0.11; REMED 0.05/0.06/-0.06; LANGIMP 0.00/0.02/0.04; SMQR 0.17/0.17/0.06 across DA/DA+/RA prompts). The paper concludes the model performed poorly at scoring classroom transcripts and that added rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted and human-rated observation scores

findings.finding_summary: For identifying highlights and missed opportunities, teachers generally did not find ChatGPT's responses insightful or relevant. The paper reports that 20-30% of responses were judged unfaithful, with model performance worse on MQI than CLASS; low scores on faithful increased from 22% to 29%, relevant from 35% to 55%, and insightful from 51% to 71% when moving from CLASS to MQI.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated feedback
findings.sample_size: n=504 evaluated items total (216 CLASS + 288 MQI)

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions to elicit student reasoning, 82% of ChatGPT's suggestions were redundant, meaning they repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript. The authors note that although many suggestions were actionable and faithful, the strong redundancy indicates limited novelty and substantial overreliance on transcript restatement.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of faithfulness, relevance, actionability, and novelty/redundancy of suggestions

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single paper with qualitative and correlational evaluation of ChatGPT rather than a randomized or causal field study. The methodology is clear, but the evidence is limited to a small sample of teacher raters and transcript segments.
impact_tier_rationale: The main findings are negative or null for teacher-coaching performance: low score correlation, unfaithful or non-insightful feedback, and 82% redundant suggestions. Reported effects are not framed as beneficial classroom impact and there are no positive outcome effect sizes to support meaningful impact.
